newsitem.title: UK: British trade unions call for budget for jobs.
newsitem.headline: British trade unions call for budget for jobs.

text.p: Britain's trade unions called on Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Thursday to serve up a budget for jobs and investment and offered a partnership to ensure high-quality work and training for the jobless.

The Trades Union Congress' budget submission welcomed the government's commitment to helping the unemployed and the planned windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities that will pay for a mass job creation programme.
Brown has pledged to unveil a first budget within two months of coming to power and make the windfall tax its centrepiece.

"The TUC is seeking partnership with the new government, as well as employers, to ensure quality jobs or training for our young people and long-term unemployed," TUC General Secretary John Monks said.

"We therefore very much welcome the windfall levy and call upon those who will pay it to recognise their social responsibilities, end their special pleading, and recall the firm backing given to the levy by the voters."
Labour, swept into a power with a landslide election victory on May 1, made a windfall tax on what it called the excess profits of privatised utilities a central theme of its campaign.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has said the tax will comfortably cover a three billion pounds programme to get 250,000 people into work.

But already, British Telecommunications Plc said it would not hesitate to launch a legal challenge if asked to pay up. And airports operator BAA said the new government was "verging on irresponsibility" by not detailing who would be hit.
The union organisation said an effective jobs programme must be supported by high quality training and widely available childcare.
Its report, which will be presented to Brown, agreed with his assertion that industry is blighted by low investment and said interest rates should stay low to promote it.
The government's 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation can be met without further monetary tightening, it said.

Since Brown has granted the Bank of England operational independence to set interest rates, the unions may be addressing the wrong audience. But the TUC expressed its fervent hope that the new monetary policy committee would remember not only its remit to deliver price stability but also to support the government's growth and employment objectives.

It said there was no case for fiscal tightening either. "Net taxes do not need to be raised to slow consumption or lower public borrowing, but if further tightening of policy is required in the medium-term this should be through higher taxes rather than higher interest rates."

Many economists agree with that assertion. Tighter monetary policy could push the pound -- already up about 17 percent in little over nine months -- higher still, raising export prices and hitting Britain's already-bruised manufacturers.

Economists and the Bank of England say the rampant parts of the economy are the services and retail sectors. They are fuelled by bubbling consumer demand and personal tax rises would be The TUC said a stable but expansionary economic climate -- something Brown promised to Britain's top business leaders on Tuesday -- would help investment.

But so too would changes to the tax regime to promote long-term holding of shares, rather than chasing a quick buck -- encouraging companies to retain profits rather than pay massive dividends to woo institutional investors.
Some experts say Brown will axe advanced corporation tax in his budget, closing a tax break for share-holding pension funds.

The TUC also said public spending on capital investment should rise over the medium-term, particularly on investment and job creating measures in housing, transport and the environment -- even though Brown has promised to keep spending on the tightest of leashes.
But it spared the government's blushes over a minimum wage, stating simply that a national floor is key to helping people into work and making work pay.
Last year, the TUC annual conference passed a motion calling for a minimum wage of 4.26 pounds an hour. Business leaders say anything above 3.50 will cost jobs and hit competitiveness.
